title: Global EbA Fund Grants 2026: Up to $500,000 for Ecosystem-Based Adaptation Projects in Developing Countries
summary: The Global EbA Fund Grants 2026 provide an important funding opportunity for organisations working to address climate change, strengthen ecosystem resilience and advance Ecosystem-based Adaptation (EbA) in vulnerable countries. For the 2026 funding cycle, the Global EbA Fund is inviting organisations to submit innovative and catalytic proposals designed to overcome systemic barriers that prevent Ecosystem-based Adaptation from being adopted, scaled and mainstreamed. The calls place particular emphasis on Small Island Developing States (SIDS) and Least Developed Countries (LDCs) , where climate vulnerability is often high while institutional, technical and financial capacity remains constrained. The 2026 calls provide two grant tracks: Small-Size Grants of up to US$250,000 and Medium-Size Grants of up to US$500,000 . Both tracks support projects of up to 24 months and seek initiatives capable of creating lasting enabling conditions for climate adaptation rather than simply financing isolated conservation activities. What Is the Global EbA Fund? The Global EbA Fund is a funding mechanism focused on creating an enabling environment for the implementation and scaling of Ecosystem-based Adaptation . Ecosystem-based Adaptation uses the conservation, restoration and sustainable management of ecosystems to help people and communities adapt to the impacts of climate change. Rather than treating climate adaptation solely as an infrastructure or technological challenge, EbA recognises the important role that healthy ecosystems can play in reducing climate vulnerability. The Fund supports innovative initiatives that address the systemic obstacles preventing EbA from being effectively adopted and expanded. These obstacles can include gaps in: Climate and environmental data Scientific evidence Technical capacity Institutional capacity Governance Policy implementation Financing Investment readiness Knowledge sharing Awareness Partnerships and collaboration According to the information provided, the Fund has been operational since 2020 and, as of June 2026, had supported 75 projects across 41 countries , with 29 projects completed and 46 at various stages of implementation . Its portfolio covers a wide range of ecosystems and landscapes, including: Coastal and marine environments Drylands Grasslands Forests Mountains Urban areas River basins Wetlands This broad portfolio demonstrates that Ecosystem-based Adaptation can be applied across different ecological, social and economic contexts. The Fund s overall objective is to finance innovative approaches capable of overcoming systemic barriers and enabling EbA to be taken up, scaled and mainstreamed. Learn More HERE Why the 2026 Global EbA Fund Call Matters Climate change is increasing pressure on communities, economies and ecosystems around the world. Rising temperatures, droughts, floods, storms, changing rainfall patterns, sea-level rise and other climate-related hazards are affecting food security, water security, livelihoods and socioeconomic development. At the same time, many ecosystems are being degraded through unsustainable resource use and other pressures. This creates a double challenge: communities become increasingly exposed to climate risks while the ecosystems that could help protect them become less capable of providing essential services. Ecosystem-based Adaptation seeks to address these interconnected challenges by strengthening the health and resilience of ecosystems while also reducing vulnerability among people. The 2026 Global EbA Fund calls are particularly relevant to Small Island Developing States and Least Developed Countries . SIDS are highly vulnerable to climate impacts because of factors such as their small land areas, remoteness and close connections between communities, oceans and ecosystems. They can face increasingly frequent and intense tropical cyclones, storm surges, heatwaves, droughts, flooding, changing precipitation patterns and sea-level rise. LDCs also face significant climate vulnerability. Their economies frequently depend heavily on climate-sensitive sectors, while limited institutional and financial capacity can make it difficult to recover from climate-related shocks or mobilise sufficient resources for adaptation. The call therefore seeks projects that do more than implement individual adaptation activities. It seeks initiatives capable of strengthening the systems, institutions, knowledge, partnerships and investment mechanisms needed to enable EbA to grow over the long term. Global EbA Fund Small-Size Grants 2026 The Small-Size Grants Call for Proposals is intended to support innovative and catalytic initiatives that address systemic barriers to scaling Ecosystem-based Adaptation. Small-Size Grant Amount The Fund will provide grants of up to US$250,000 per project . The provided call information indicates that the Small-Size Grants track will support 10 grants , with projects lasting between 18 and 24 months . The official webpage specifies a maximum project duration of 24 months. Small-Size Grants Deadline Applications for the Small-Size Grants can be submitted through the online platform from: 28 September to 26 October 2026 The application deadline is 26 October 2026 . The call was officially launched on 24 August 2026 . Click HERE to download the Small-size Call for Proposals Document. What the Small-Size Grants Will Support The Small-Size Grants call is looking for projects that address upstream or systemic barriers preventing the uptake and scaling of Ecosystem-based Adaptation. Successful proposals should contribute to one or more areas such as: 1. Strengthening Institutional and Technical Capacity Projects can address institutional or technical limitations that prevent organisations, governments and other stakeholders from effectively implementing EbA. This could include initiatives that improve technical expertise, institutional systems, planning capacity or decision-making processes. 2. Improving Data and Evidence Strong evidence is essential for convincing policymakers, investors and other stakeholders to support adaptation approaches. The Fund therefore welcomes projects that generate, improve or apply quality data and evidence to resolve specific barriers to EbA implementation and investment. 3. Building Knowledge and Learning Networks Projects can strengthen systematic knowledge exchange, learning networks and communities of practice that enable practitioners and decision-makers to learn from successful EbA approaches. 4. Improving Investment Readiness The call encourages initiatives that prepare projects and concepts capable of attracting larger-scale climate financing. This can include developing investable project pipelines, strengthening financial models and preparing scalable concepts that can eventually move beyond small grant funding. 5. Supporting Innovative EbA Technologies Projects may adapt or scale tested technological solutions for particular socio-ecological systems. The emphasis is on technologies that can generate useful lessons for practitioners and decision-makers and contribute to broader EbA uptake. 6. Conducting Applied and Functional Research The Fund is interested in practical research that addresses specific obstacles to EbA implementation or investment. Research should therefore have a clear application and contribute to solving real-world adaptation challenges. 7. Creating Synergies With Other Initiatives Applicants are encouraged to work with existing Ecosystem-based Adaptation and Nature-based Solution initiatives where this can generate operational synergies, strengthen collaboration and create opportunities for co-financing. These areas are explicitly highlighted in the Small-Size Grants call. Key Requirements for Small-Size Grant Proposals A successful Small-Size Grant proposal must demonstrate that the project is genuinely focused on Ecosystem-based Adaptation and has the potential to create an enabling environment for its uptake and scaling. Projects must: Qualify as Ecosystem-based Adaptation. Have catalytic and innovative potential. Clearly identify the climate impacts being addressed. Explain how the proposed intervention will address those impacts. Fall under no more than one Strategic Objective and no more than two Action Pillars of the Global EbA Fund. Be global, thematic or focused on ODA-eligible countries. Request no more than US$250,000 . Have a duration of no more than 24 months . Build on existing work rather than being an entirely standalone initiative. Demonstrate how results will continue after Fund support ends. Partner with local institutions and organisations. Demonstrate relevant experience in the proposed area of work. Incorporate local communities, Indigenous Knowledge and gender perspectives. Be led by legally recognised entities. Meet the Fund s due-diligence requirements. Social and Environmental Considerations The Global EbA Fund places significant importance on ensuring that climate adaptation projects are socially inclusive and environmentally responsible. Proposals should therefore incorporate: Gender responsiveness Meaningful local participation Respect for Indigenous Peoples rights Environmental and social safeguards Equitable benefit-sharing Prevention of maladaptation Use of local, Indigenous and traditional knowledge where appropriate Applicants should clearly identify the communities and groups that will benefit from the project and explain how those groups will participate in the initiative. The evaluation framework also specifically considers the involvement of women, youth, Indigenous Peoples and other marginalised groups. Where Indigenous Peoples may be affected, Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC) is expected to be upheld. Sustainability and Long-Term Impact The Fund is not simply looking for projects that produce short-term outputs during the grant period. Applicants must demonstrate how their work will remain viable after the funding period. A strong proposal should therefore explain: How local ownership will be established. How institutions will continue the work. How project results can be replicated. How successful approaches can be scaled. How knowledge and capacities will be retained. How the initiative connects to relevant national and global policies. How partnerships will continue after the project ends. How additional financing can be mobilised. The Fund specifically evaluates sustainability, including replication, upscaling and links with national and global policies such as Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) and National Adaptation Plans (NAPs) . Learn More and Apply HERE Global EbA Fund Medium-Size Grants 2026 Alongside the Small-Size Grants, the Global EbA Fund has opened a Medium-Size Grants Call for Proposals . This track provides larger funding for collaborative and innovative initiatives focused on strategic scaling and global influence. Medium-Size Grant Amount Each Medium-Size Grant can provide up to US$500,000 . Projects can run for up to 24 months . Medium-Size Grants Deadline Applications will be accepted through the online platform from: 12 October to 16 November 2026 The application deadline is 16 November 2026 . The Medium-Size Grants call was officially launched on 24 August 2026 . Click HERE to download the Medium-size Call for Proposals Document. Medium-Size Grants General Track: Strategic Scaling and Global Influence The Medium-Size Grants General Track is aimed at proposals that demonstrate collaborative and innovative approaches to advancing Ecosystem-based Adaptation. The focus is on projects that can address systemic barriers to scalability while contributing to broader learning and policy dialogue. Projects that strengthen enabling environments and integrate EbA into national frameworks are particularly relevant. The call identifies three priority themes. 1. Innovative Finance Solutions for EbA This theme focuses on partnerships with private-sector actors, financiers, innovators, adaptation practitioners and local champions to unlock private capital and blended finance for Ecosystem-based Adaptation. The underlying objective is to help EbA evolve beyond small-scale or subsistence-level activities and develop business models that are commercially viable, scalable and capable of creating incentives for conservation. Applicants working in this area should demonstrate how their proposed approach can help overcome financing barriers and make EbA more attractive to investors and other financing partners. 2. EbA for Human Development and Security This theme explores the connection between climate resilience, human development and security , particularly in fragile and conflict-affected contexts. Projects should identify specific policy, regulatory, financial or awareness barriers that prevent investment in EbA in high-risk areas. The Fund is interested in preventive and community-designed interventions that can: Protect vulnerable populations. Reduce exposure to climate-related risks. Strengthen resilience. Reduce natural-resource-related tensions. Strengthen social cohesion. Connect adaptation with humanitarian action. Support development and peacebuilding objectives. Strong proposals should establish a measurable pathway showing how targeted EbA investment can contribute to reducing climate-induced fragility. 3. People-Nature-Climate-Land Synergies The third theme focuses on strengthening connections between climate change, biodiversity, sustainable land management and disaster risk reduction. The Fund invites proposals led by organisations that actively collaborate with national governments to strengthen operational links between the UNFCCC, Convention on Biological Diversity, UNCCD, Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction and other relevant international environmental commitments. The objective is to connect existing commitments, actors, tools and financing opportunities so countries and communities can reduce duplication and use integrated interventions to achieve multiple environmental and development outcomes. Who Can Apply for the Global EbA Fund Grants? The Global EbA Fund is designed primarily for organisations , not individual applicants. Eligible organisation types include: Non-governmental organisations (NGOs) International non-governmental organisations (INGOs) Intergovernmental organisations (IGOs) Community-based organisations (CBOs) Indigenous Peoples Organisations Universities and other academic institutions Research institutes and think tanks Private-sector companies , subject to the Fund s conditions Consortia of organisations collaborating to create greater impact around EbA Government entities can participate in consortia, provided that they do not receive funding from the Global EbA Fund . A consortium application must clearly identify its lead organisation, which becomes the responsible contract party if the proposal is successful. The same broad organisational eligibility structure applies to the Medium-Size Grants. Learn More and Apply HERE Local Partnerships and the Role of Local Organisations One of the important features of the Global EbA Fund is its emphasis on local ownership. For country-level activities, the call information provided states that a consortium involving one or more local organisations is required, with at least 25% of the project budget allocated to local partners , subject to compliance with applicable standards and due-diligence requirements. These partnerships should demonstrate: Capacity transfer Shared decision-making Long-term institutional strengthening Local ownership Knowledge transfer Sustainability Meaningful community participation This requirement is particularly important for organisations applying from outside the country where project activities will take place. What Makes a Strong Global EbA Fund Proposal? The Fund s evaluation criteria provide applicants with a useful indication of what reviewers will be looking for. Ecosystem-Based Adaptation — 30% The proposal must clearly demonstrate that it is an EbA intervention and explain how it will reduce vulnerability or increase the resilience of human communities to climate change. Applicants should clearly identify: The main climate hazards. The climate risks involved. The affected communities. Ecosystem vulnerabilities. The ecosystem services involved. How the proposed intervention will reduce vulnerability. The proposal should establish a convincing connection between ecosystem management and climate adaptation outcomes. Innovative and Catalytic Contribution — 30% Innovation and catalytic potential are also worth 30% of the evaluation. The Fund wants interventions capable of producing systemic change. Examples could include initiatives that: Influence policy. Address institutional capacity gaps. Develop new financing mechanisms. Improve governance. Strengthen investment readiness. Demonstrate approaches that can be replicated elsewhere. Test approaches in new contexts. The key question is not simply whether the project is innovative, but whether it can help trigger broader transformation in how EbA is implemented or financed. Sustainability — 20% Sustainability accounts for 20% of the evaluation. Applicants need to explain how activities and results will continue beyond the grant period, including opportunities for replication and upscaling. Proposals should also demonstrate connections to relevant national and international policies and synergies with other initiatives. Institutional Arrangements — 20% Institutional arrangements account for another 20% . The applicant organisation should have: An appropriate organisational structure. Adequate financial capacity. Strong internal controls. Qualified and dedicated staff. Relevant technical expertise. Previous experience implementing projects of similar scope and complexity. This means applicants should not focus exclusively on the technical idea. They must also demonstrate that their organisation has the capacity to responsibly manage the proposed funding and deliver the project. Theory of Change, Logical Framework and SMART Indicators A strong application should have a clear and logical Theory of Change . The Fund expects the results chain to demonstrate how proposed activities will lead to outputs and outcomes that create an enabling environment for reducing identified climate risks. The project design should include: A logical and coherent results chain. Feasible activities. A realistic implementation timeline. SMART indicators. Appropriate data sources. Defined reporting intervals. A budget that corresponds logically with activities and timelines. Applicants must also use the Global EbA Fund s Core Indicator Framework . At least three relevant indicators from the Core Indicator Framework must be incorporated into the project s logical framework. Existing Work Is Important A key eligibility requirement is that the proposed project must be built on or based on existing work . Applicants should therefore avoid presenting an entirely disconnected idea with no evidence of previous activity, experience or groundwork. A stronger proposal can demonstrate: Previous pilot activities. Existing partnerships. Prior research. Community engagement. Existing institutional relationships. Previous data or evidence. Lessons learned. Existing projects that can be scaled or replicated. This helps demonstrate that the proposed investment can move an existing concept toward greater impact rather than starting from zero. Application Documents Applicants should carefully prepare the required application package before the relevant submission window opens. For the Small-Size Grants , the application package includes: Applicant Declaration Co-applicant Mandate Small-Size Grants Application Form Project Proposal Budget Template Due Diligence and Financial Capacity Questionnaire The Fund specifically advises applicants to review the Grants Procedure Manual before developing and submitting their proposal. The Medium-Size Grants application package similarly includes: Applicant Declaration Co-applicant Mandate Medium-Size Grants Application Form Project Proposal Budget Template Due Diligence and Financial Capacity Questionnaire How to Apply for the Global EbA Fund Grants 2026 Applications must be submitted through the Global EbA Fund s online platform . Applicants should not simply complete the downloadable application form and assume that submitting the document itself constitutes an application. The Fund explicitly states that the application form is intended for drafting purposes and that applications must ultimately be submitted through the online platform. The Fund strongly recommends that applicants: Download and review the relevant application materials. Read the Grants Procedure Manual carefully. Review the eligibility requirements. Identify the appropriate Strategic Objective and Action Pillars. Develop the project s Theory of Change. Develop the logical framework and SMART indicators. Identify at least three relevant Core Indicators. Establish the climate hazards and risks the project will address. Demonstrate the project s EbA approach. Develop a realistic implementation plan. Prepare the project budget. Establish local partnerships where required. Complete the required due-diligence documentation. Draft the application offline. Transfer the completed application to the online platform. Submit before the applicable deadline. For the Small-Size Grants, the online submission link is expected to be shared on the Small-Size Grants webpage on 28 September 2026 . For the Medium-Size Grants, the online submission link is expected to be shared on the Medium-Size Grants webpage on 12 October 2026 . Global EbA Fund 2026: Important Deadlines at a Glance Grant Track Funding Project Duration Application Period Deadline Small-Size Grants Up to US$250,000 Up to 24 months 28 September–26 October 2026 26 October 2026 Medium-Size Grants Up to US$500,000 Up to 24 months 12 October–16 November 2026 16 November 2026 Both calls were officially launched on 24 August 2026 . Small-Size vs Medium-Size Global EbA Fund Grants Although both funding opportunities are part of the Global EbA Fund, applicants should carefully consider which track best matches the scale and ambition of their project. Small-Size Grants The Small-Size Grants provide up to US$250,000 and are particularly focused on catalytic interventions that overcome barriers to EbA uptake and scaling. They are well suited to projects addressing issues such as: Institutional and technical capacity. Evidence and data gaps. Knowledge exchange. Investment readiness. Applied research. Innovative EbA technologies. Synergies with existing EbA and Nature-based Solution initiatives. Medium-Size Grants The Medium-Size Grants provide up to US$500,000 and have a stronger emphasis on strategic scaling and global influence. The General Track highlights: Innovative finance for EbA. EbA for human development and security. People-nature-climate-land synergies. National policy integration. Global learning. Policy dialogue. Collaborative approaches to systemic scaling. Both tracks require projects to qualify as EbA, demonstrate innovation and catalytic potential, work with local partners and show how project results can be sustained beyond the funding period. Who Should Consider Applying? The Global EbA Fund 2026 calls may be particularly relevant to organisations working at the intersection of: Climate change adaptation Ecosystem restoration Biodiversity conservation Nature-based Solutions Sustainable land management Water security Food security Climate finance Environmental governance Climate policy Community development Indigenous knowledge Applied environmental research Investment readiness Sustainable technologies Disaster risk reduction Human development and resilience Organisations should, however, ensure that their proposal addresses the Fund s specific emphasis on Ecosystem-based Adaptation and systemic barriers to its uptake, investment, scaling or mainstreaming rather than presenting a conventional conservation or development project without a clear EbA connection. Important Tips for Applicants Before applying, organisations should pay close attention to the following: Make the climate-adaptation connection explicit Do not assume that reviewers will automatically understand how an environmental project contributes to climate adaptation. Clearly identify the climate hazard, vulnerability and adaptation pathway. Demonstrate systemic impact The Fund is looking for projects capable of changing systems, institutions, policies, financing mechanisms, knowledge or capacity. Explain what barrier exists and how your project will help remove it. Build on existing work Use evidence from previous projects, research, partnerships, pilots and community engagement to demonstrate that the proposal is grounded in experience. Prioritise local ownership Meaningful participation from local organisations and communities should be integrated into project design rather than treated as an afterthought. Make gender and social inclusion substantive Explain how women, youth, Indigenous Peoples and marginalised groups will participate and benefit. Where relevant, incorporate gender-disaggregated information and Indigenous or traditional knowledge. Think beyond the grant period Explain who will maintain the results, how activities will be financed after the grant, how knowledge will be retained and how successful approaches could be replicated or scaled. Prepare early Because applications must be submitted online and involve several supporting documents, applicants should prepare their materials well before the submission window. Read the Grants Procedure Manual The Global EbA Fund strongly recommends reviewing the Grants Procedure Manual before developing a proposal. Conclusion The Global EbA Fund Grants 2026 present a significant funding opportunity for organisations seeking to strengthen climate resilience through Ecosystem-based Adaptation. With grants of up to US$250,000 under the Small-Size Grants track and up to US$500,000 under the Medium-Size Grants track , the calls are designed to support initiatives that can address the institutional, technical, financial, knowledge and governance barriers preventing EbA from being scaled. The opportunity is particularly relevant to organisations working in ODA-eligible Small Island Developing States and Least Developed Countries , although other ODA-eligible countries may also be considered when proposals demonstrate exceptional ambition and unique opportunities for scaling EbA. Applicants should remember that the Fund is not simply seeking conventional environmental projects. Strong proposals should clearly demonstrate an Ecosystem-based Adaptation approach, a defined climate-risk pathway, innovative and catalytic potential, meaningful social inclusion, strong institutional arrangements, local partnerships and a credible plan for sustainability and replication . For organisations preparing applications, early planning will be essential. The Small-Size Grants deadline is 26 October 2026 , while the Medium-Size Grants deadline is 16 November 2026 . Applicants should carefully review the relevant call documents, Grants Procedure Manual, eligibility requirements, evaluation criteria and Core Indicator Framework before submitting their proposals. Overall, the Global EbA Fund offers an opportunity not only to obtain project financing but also to help build the policies, institutions, partnerships, evidence, investment mechanisms and local capacities needed to make climate adaptation more sustainable and effective for both people and nature . title: Commonwealth Women’s Forum 2026: Pre-Registration Now Open for Women’s Leadership and Gender Equality Forum
summary: The Commonwealth Women’s Forum (CWF) 2026 is inviting prospective participants to express their interest in attending a major forum focused on advancing women’s leadership, economic empowerment, gender equality, and women’s rights. The forum will bring together participants interested in contributing to discussions around some of the most pressing issues affecting women and girls, including leadership, economic opportunity, violence against women and girls, climate change, and accountability for gender equality. Key Discussion Areas The Commonwealth Women’s Forum 2026 will focus on five major themes: Women in leadership Women’s economic empowerment Ending violence against women and girls Gender and climate change Accountability for gender equality Who Should Consider Participating? The pre-registration form is designed for prospective participants who have an interest, experience, expertise, or perspective that can contribute to the Forum’s thematic discussions. Participants may come from different sectors, including: Government institutions Intergovernmental organisations Non-governmental organisations Non-profit organisations Private-sector organisations Women’s rights and gender-equality initiatives Organisations working on climate change, economic empowerment, leadership, or social development Applicants are asked to provide their organisation, designation/job title, organisation type, and a brief statement explaining their motivation for participating and how their experience or expertise could contribute to the Forum . The motivation statement must be no more than 600 characters . Important: This Is a Pre-Registration/Expression of Interest Submitting the form does not guarantee registration or participation in the Commonwealth Women’s Forum 2026. The form is intended to help capture expressions of interest and support planning and organisation of the Forum. Eligible applicants will receive further information about confirmation of participation and registration or accreditation procedures at a later stage. Applicants should therefore understand that completing the form is an initial expression of interest rather than confirmation of attendance. The Forum Is Self-Funded One of the most important points for prospective participants is that the Commonwealth Women’s Forum 2026 is a self-funded event . Delegates who are confirmed to participate will be responsible for covering their own: International or domestic travel Accommodation Visa expenses, where applicable Travel and medical insurance Other personal or logistical expenses associated with attending the Forum The Commonwealth Secretariat will not provide travel funding, arrange travel, book accommodation, or provide associated logistical support for delegates attending the Forum. Prospective participants should therefore consider their ability to finance their participation before submitting an expression of interest. Data and Confirmation Requirements Before submitting the form, applicants must confirm that the information they have provided is accurate and complete to the best of their knowledge. Applicants must also acknowledge that participation in CWF 2026 is self-funded . In addition, the form requests applicants’ consent for their personal data to be processed for the purposes of administering the Commonwealth Women’s Forum. How to Prepare a Strong Expression of Interest Although the form only requests a short motivation statement, applicants should use the limited space strategically. A strong response could briefly demonstrate: Why the Commonwealth Women’s Forum is relevant to their work or interests. Which thematic area they are most connected to. Relevant professional, academic, community, advocacy, or leadership experience. What perspective or contribution they could bring to the Forum. How participation could support their ongoing work in advancing gender equality. Because the statement is limited to 600 characters , applicants should avoid lengthy background information and focus on their most relevant experience and contribution. APPLY HERE Conclusion The Commonwealth Women’s Forum 2026 provides an opportunity for prospective participants to express their interest in engaging with discussions on women’s leadership, economic empowerment, violence against women and girls, gender and climate change, and accountability for gender equality. The Forum is open to prospective participants from a range of professional and organisational backgrounds, but participation is not guaranteed through pre-registration and the event is self-funded . Individuals interested in attending should carefully consider the financial requirements and provide a focused, relevant motivation statement when submitting their expression of interest. title: Born This Way Foundation Youth Advisory Board 2027–2028: Applications Open for Young People Worldwide
summary: Young people aged 15 to 24 who are passionate about their communities, youth engagement, social change, and making a positive difference have an opportunity to apply for the Born This Way Foundation Youth Advisory Board 2027–2028 cohort . Applications are now open for young people who want to contribute their ideas and perspectives to research, programs, campaigns, and community initiatives. Members of the Youth Advisory Board will also have the opportunity to serve as ambassadors for the Foundation s work in their communities and beyond. The opportunity is open to applicants from around the globe , while the Foundation is also specifically seeking applicants from Brazil, Canada, Singapore, South Africa, Spain, the United Kingdom, and the United States . Applications must be submitted by September 30, 2026, at 11:59 PM ET . About the Born This Way Foundation Youth Advisory Board The Born This Way Foundation has been shaped and guided by young people since its founding nearly 15 years ago. Youth participation is therefore an important part of the Foundation s approach to its work. The Youth Advisory Board provides young people with an opportunity to contribute directly to initiatives connected to the Foundation s mission. Rather than simply being recipients of youth-focused programs, members can contribute their perspectives and ideas to help inform the organization s research, programs, and campaigns. Youth Advisory Board members also serve as ambassadors for the Foundation s work, allowing them to share and promote its mission within their communities and beyond. The newly announced cohort will cover the 2027–2028 period. Applications Are Now Open for the 2027–2028 Cohort The Foundation is inviting young people between 15 and 24 years old to apply. The opportunity may be particularly relevant to young people who: Want to become more involved in their communities Have ideas about issues affecting young people Are interested in youth leadership and participation Want to contribute to research, programs, or campaigns Are interested in social impact and community engagement Want to represent young people s perspectives Are interested in working with other young people Want to contribute to creating a kinder and braver world Applicants do not necessarily need to have extensive professional experience. The announcement emphasizes young people who are eager to become involved in their communities and beyond. What Does the Youth Advisory Board Do? Youth Advisory Board members have an important role in helping shape and support the Foundation s work. According to the announcement, members play a key role in helping the organization carry out research, programs, and campaigns that are central to its mission. 1. Contribute to Research Youth Advisory Board members can bring their perspectives and experiences to research activities. The involvement of young people can help ensure that youth-related research takes into consideration the perspectives and experiences of the people it seeks to understand or support. 2. Contribute to Programs Board members also play a role in the Foundation s programs. Their ideas and perspectives can help inform programs and initiatives intended to engage and support young people. 3. Support Campaigns Campaigns are another important area of Youth Advisory Board involvement. Members can contribute youth perspectives to campaigns connected to the Foundation s mission and help ensure that youth voices are represented. 4. Serve as Ambassadors Youth Advisory Board members also serve as ambassadors for the Foundation s work. This means that members can help communicate the Foundation s work within their communities and beyond, extending youth engagement beyond the board itself. Who Should Consider Applying? The opportunity is designed for young people who want to participate actively in their communities and contribute their ideas to work involving young people. A prospective applicant may be particularly well suited to the opportunity if they have an interest in areas such as: Youth leadership Community development Social change Advocacy Youth participation Campaigns and communications Research Community organizing Social impact Youth-focused initiatives However, the source does not provide a specific list of academic qualifications, professional experience requirements, or required degrees. The central eligibility information provided is that applicants should be 15 to 24 years old and interested in getting involved in their communities and beyond. What Is the Age Requirement? The opportunity is specifically aimed at young people aged: 15 to 24 years old Anyone considering applying should make sure they meet the age requirement before submitting an application. The source does not provide additional age-related conditions beyond the stated 15–24 age range. Are There Specific Educational Requirements? The announcement does not identify a minimum educational qualification. It does not state that applicants must: Hold a university degree Be university students Have completed secondary school Have professional qualifications Have previous employment experience Instead, the opportunity focuses on young people and their interest in becoming involved in their communities and beyond. Applicants should therefore carefully follow the actual questions and requirements in the official application rather than assuming that a particular academic qualification is necessary. Are There Specific Professional Experience Requirements? No specific professional experience requirement is stated in the provided announcement. The Youth Advisory Board is intended to involve young people in the Foundation s research, programs, campaigns, and community engagement. Applicants can therefore focus on communicating their interests, experiences, ideas, community involvement, and motivation. Examples of relevant experiences could include community activities, volunteering, youth initiatives, student organizations, advocacy activities, creative projects, campaigns, or other forms of community engagement, although the source does not state that any of these are mandatory. Click HERE to read more. Information Sessions for Applicants Prospective applicants are also encouraged to attend an information session. These sessions are designed to give interested young people an opportunity to ask questions about the Youth Advisory Board and hear directly from a current Youth Advisory Board member about their experience. The sessions are 60 minutes long . The Foundation has stated that the sessions will not be recorded , and interested applicants are encouraged to RSVP for only one session because spaces are limited. Information Session 1 August 25, 2026 at 11:00 AM ET Status: Session Full Information Session 2 September 1, 2026 at 11:00 AM ET Registration is available through the designated information-session registration page. Information Session 3 September 9, 2026 at 7:00 PM ET Registration is available through the designated information-session registration page. Information Session 4 September 15, 2026 at 7:00 PM ET The announcement states that this session is almost full . Because spaces are limited, applicants who want to attend should register as early as possible. Application Deadline The Youth Advisory Board application deadline is: September 30, 2026, at 11:59 PM ET Applicants should make sure their application is submitted before the deadline. Waiting until the final day can create unnecessary problems if an applicant encounters technical difficulties or needs additional time to review their responses. APPLY NOW How Applicants Can Prepare a Strong Application Although the provided announcement does not publish a formal scoring rubric, applicants can use the purpose of the Youth Advisory Board to guide their preparation. 1. Think about your community involvement Consider how you have participated in your community. This does not necessarily have to involve a formal organization. Community involvement can take many forms, and applicants should focus on experiences that demonstrate their willingness to contribute and engage with others. 2. Explain your interests Think about the issues affecting young people that matter to you. Be specific about what motivates you and why you would like to contribute to the Foundation s work. 3. Share your ideas The Youth Advisory Board is intended to be shaped and guided by young people. Applicants should therefore consider what perspectives, ideas, or experiences they could bring to the board. 4. Demonstrate your willingness to participate Being a Youth Advisory Board member involves contributing to research, programs, campaigns, and the Foundation s broader work. Applicants should demonstrate that they are genuinely interested in participating rather than simply seeking a title or credential. 5. Be authentic The Foundation says it is looking forward to learning more about applicants, their ideas, and how they hope to help build a kinder and braver world. Applicants should therefore allow their personality, experiences, interests, and aspirations to come through in their responses. It is a youth-focused advisory opportunity through which young people contribute to the Foundation s research, programs, campaigns, and community work while also serving as ambassadors for its work. Who can apply? Young people aged 15 to 24 can apply. Can applicants from outside the United States apply? Yes. The Foundation states that it welcomes applicants from around the globe . title: Nike Community Impact Fund 2026: Supporting Local Organizations That Expand Youth Access to Sport and Play
summary: Explore the Nike Community Impact Fund 2026, including its eligible locations, funding priorities, regional award amounts, application process, selection criteria, deadlines, and practical application guidance. The Nike Community Impact Fund 2026 supports community-based organizations working to ensure that more children and young people can participate in sport, play and physical activity. The initiative concentrates on communities surrounding Nike offices, logistics centres, manufacturing facilities and other locations where Nike employees live and work. Through this initiative, Nike invests in local nonprofit organizations and schools that are creating positive and lasting change for young people. Its central purpose is to make sport and play more accessible, particularly for children who face financial, social, cultural, physical or other barriers to participation. What makes the initiative distinctive is its employee-led selection model. Nike employees do not merely contribute funding; they participate directly in reviewing applications and recommending the organizations that should receive support. This neighbourhood-focused approach allows local knowledge to influence funding decisions. According to the official Nike Community Impact Fund page , applications generally begin in January in participating communities. Local organizations are normally notified about decisions, and approved funding is distributed, by the end of May. Important 2026 Application Status As of August 28, 2026, the published 2026 application rounds have closed. Some regional partners have already announced successful organizations or distributed their 2026 awards. There is no single worldwide application deadline. Every participating location works through a designated regional partner, and application dates, award amounts, legal-status requirements and project conditions can vary. For example: The Pacific Northwest application closed on February 17, 2026, at 5:00 p.m. Pacific Time. The Belgium application closed on February 12, 2026. The United States application portal administered by Charities Aid Foundation of America is no longer available. The Toronto partner has announced the 13 organizations selected for support. The Nike overview directs eligible organizations to look for application opportunities beginning in January. Dates for the next application cycle have not yet been published on Nike’s main initiative page. Prospective applicants should monitor the official page and the appropriate regional partner, particularly around January. What Is the Nike Community Impact Fund? The Nike Community Impact Fund, commonly referred to as NCIF, is designed to strengthen community-level efforts that use sport and physical activity to improve the lives of children and young people. The initiative is based on the understanding that participation in quality sport and play can help young people: Develop confidence and resilience. Build communication, leadership and teamwork skills. Improve their physical and mental well-being. Form stronger connections with their peers and communities. Gain access to positive coaches, mentors and role models. Overcome social isolation and exclusion. Participate in safe, structured and inclusive activities. Discover opportunities that may otherwise remain inaccessible. Rather than applying one uniform model to every location, Nike works through local institutions that understand the legal, social and administrative conditions of their respective communities. How the Nike Community Impact Fund Works The initiative generally follows a five-stage process: Regional applications open Starting around January, organizations operating in participating communities can submit applications through their designated regional partner. Applications undergo an eligibility review The regional administrator confirms whether the applicant has an acceptable legal status, operates in an eligible area and proposes activities aligned with the relevant funding priorities. Nike employees receive application-review training Volunteer committees include Nike employees from offices, logistics centres, Air Manufacturing and Innovation sites, and other local operations. Local committees assess the proposals Committee members use their knowledge of local needs and communities to review applications and recommend projects for support. Applicants receive decisions Nike’s main timetable indicates that applicants are generally notified and approved funding is distributed by the end of May. Certain regional schedules may vary. Applicants do not need to know or obtain the support of a Nike employee before applying. The Pacific Northwest frequently asked questions explicitly confirm that knowing a Nike employee is not an application requirement. Eligible Nike Community Impact Fund Locations The current Nike initiative page identifies the following participating communities: Country Eligible community or region Regional partner The Netherlands Amsterdam, Amersfoort, Hilversum and Utrecht King Baudouin Foundation Belgium Antwerp, Limburg and Flemish Brabant King Baudouin Foundation United States Atlanta, Georgia Charities Aid Foundation of America United States Mid-South/Memphis, Tennessee Charities Aid Foundation of America United States Portland, Oregon and the Pacific Northwest Oregon Community Foundation United States St. Louis, Missouri Charities Aid Foundation of America Canada Toronto Jamaal Magloire Foundation The initiative is therefore not open to organizations from every country. An applicant must operate in, and ordinarily propose a project benefiting, one of the participating communities. Who Can Apply? Nike’s main initiative page describes the intended applicants as local nonprofit organizations and schools that are creating lasting community change and making play possible for young people. However, exact legal requirements differ by location. Pacific Northwest Requirements Under the official 2026 Pacific Northwest guidelines , applications were accepted from: Organizations recognized as 501(c)(3) public charities. Federally recognized Indian Tribes under IRC Section 7871. Government entities. Organizations without their own eligible tax-exempt status when applying through an appropriately qualified fiscal sponsor. A project had to serve at least one of the following areas: Multnomah County, Oregon. Clackamas County, Oregon. Washington County, Oregon. Yamhill County, Oregon. Columbia County, Oregon. Linn County, Oregon. Benton County, Oregon. Marion County, Oregon. Polk County, Oregon. Clark County, Washington. An organization waiting to receive nonprofit status could not apply without an eligible fiscal sponsor. Belgium Requirements The official Belgium call document accepted applications from nonprofit associations, nongovernmental organizations and clubs operating in Antwerp, Limburg or Flemish Brabant. The proposed project had to: Encourage vulnerable children and young people up to 21 years old to move, play or participate in sport. Be a concrete local initiative rather than a commercial project. Explain how the activities would remove barriers to participation. Demonstrate accessible delivery arrangements. Seek a lasting effect instead of being limited to a one-time activity. Identify measurable quantitative and qualitative results. Begin implementation no later than September 2026. Aim to operate for approximately 12 months. Schools and local authorities could participate as project partners, but they could not submit an application directly under the Belgium call. The application had to be led by an eligible nonprofit organization or nongovernmental organization. The Netherlands Requirements The Netherlands regional page focuses on local organizations helping to advance youth sport in Amsterdam, Amersfoort, Hilversum and Utrecht. Organizations must review the regional selection criteria before applying because eligibility, documentation and project requirements are administered through the King Baudouin Foundation rather than through one universal Nike application. Toronto Requirements Applications for Toronto are administered through the Jamaal Magloire Foundation. Its current Nike Community Impact Fund page confirms that 13 organizations have been selected and that support ranging from $5,000 to $15,000 was awarded for initiatives providing young people with positive experiences in sport and physical activity. The Toronto page is presently displaying the selected recipients rather than accepting new submissions. Funding Priorities While detailed criteria vary among regions, competitive projects generally need to show how they will provide meaningful and inclusive opportunities for young people to participate in sport, active play or other forms of physical activity. For the Pacific Northwest, all 2026 awards were directed toward projects that get more children active. Particular priority was placed on organizations that: Provide quality coaching. Increase the participation of girls in sport and physical activity. Address social barriers that keep young people from participating. Intentionally serve communities of colour. Have boards and staff that represent the communities being served. Respond to a clearly demonstrated local need. Use a creative approach or an established method with evidence of effectiveness. Present clear objectives and a realistic sustainability plan. Submit a reasonable and proportionate project budget. Receive support through partnerships, financial contributions or in-kind assistance. Have not received support from the initiative during the previous 24 months. Serving children with higher levels of need can make an application more compelling. However, the Pacific Northwest guidance explains that schools serving a general population can still apply if the proposed project is innovative, addresses an important need and demonstrates strong community support. Barriers That Projects May Address The Belgium guidance gives useful examples of the obstacles that may prevent young people from participating in sport and play. These include: Poverty or financial hardship. Language barriers. Educational or learning disadvantages. Cultural differences. Refugee or migration backgrounds. Mental-health challenges. Behavioural difficulties. Physical or intellectual disabilities. Inaccessible facilities. Transportation or mobility limitations. Lack of equipment. Inappropriate opening hours. Complicated registration procedures. Limited access to qualified coaches. Activities that are not adapted to participants’ language or learning needs. Applicants should explain not only that a barrier exists, but also how the proposed activities will practically reduce or remove it. Examples of Relevant Community Projects The Belgium call offered several examples of activities that could align with its objectives: Mobile sport or circus activities delivered in underserved neighbourhoods. Football initiatives that combine sport with homework assistance. Programs that train young participants to become assistant coaches. Sporting activities for young people affected by domestic or family violence. Training for participants aged 16 and above to become community coaches. Skateboarding lessons for autistic children in a low-stimulation environment. The 2026 Pacific Northwest awards provide further practical examples, including: After-school sport for low-income middle-school students. Outdoor recreation for underrepresented young people. Physical activities for young people experiencing homelessness. Inclusive summer camps for participants with intellectual or developmental disabilities. Girls’ sport participation through free, culturally responsive training. Youth bicycle camps. Community football, baseball, softball and soccer programs. Recreation opportunities for foster youth. Therapeutic recreation. Movement and dance workshops. Sport-based mentoring and leadership development. These examples should be treated as guidance rather than a fixed list. A project can use any suitable sport or physical activity if it responds to a genuine local need and satisfies the applicable regional criteria. Regional Award Amounts There is no universal award amount across all participating locations. Pacific Northwest The 2026 Pacific Northwest awards ranged from $5,000 to $25,000 per organization . The Oregon Community Foundation states that Nike employees work with the foundation to award at least $550,000 annually in the Metropolitan Portland region, Northern Willamette Valley and southwest Washington. The 2026 award list records 29 awards totalling $550,000. Belgium Selected Belgium projects could request: Up to €6,000 per project . Funding from a total available budget of €140,000 . Co-financing was considered an advantage, although the guidance did not state that it was mandatory. The Netherlands The Netherlands regional page states that selected projects could receive between €5,000 and €20,000 . Toronto The Jamaal Magloire Foundation reports awards displayed as ranging from $5,000 to $15,000 for the selected Toronto organizations. Applicants should never assume that an amount published for one location applies to another. The appropriate regional rules must be consulted before preparing a budget. Activities Not Supported Under the Pacific Northwest Rules The Pacific Northwest guidelines exclude the following requests: Assistance provided directly to individuals. Scholarships, stipends, fellowships or personal financial assistance. Individual or group travel. Research projects. Fundraising-event sponsorship. Elite or private sport camps, teams or programs. Standalone one-day events, unless they are the culmination of a wider program. Endowments or memorial funds. Organizational budget deficits. Fundraising activities. Religious programs without a secular and community-focused purpose. Lobbying, political or fraternal activities. Most capital projects, unless the requested award would provide the final funding needed. Projects or events taking place before the award is distributed. Projects outside the designated geographic area. Organizations that discriminate based on age, race, ethnicity, political affiliation, religion, sexual orientation, gender, gender identity, disability or national origin. Organizations that received support from the fund during the preceding two years. The exclusions above come from the Pacific Northwest rules. Other locations may impose different or additional restrictions. 2026 Regional Timeline General Nike Process Applications generally begin: January. Employee review and recommendation process: following the application period. Applicant notification and disbursement: by the end of May. Pacific Northwest Application opened: January 8, 2026. Information session: January 21, 2026. Application deadline: February 17, 2026, at 5:00 p.m. Pacific Time. Award distribution: week of May 25, 2026. Current status: closed. Belgium Call opened: December 18, 2025. Application deadline: February 12, 2026. Selection announcement: mid-May 2026. Project implementation required to begin no later than September 2026. Intended project duration: approximately 12 months. Current status: closed. Applicants interested in a future round should not rely on these dates as the schedule for the next cycle. They should wait for a new official notice. How Applications Are Evaluated The central selection model combines formal assessment with local knowledge. Nike employees serving on review committees receive training before assessing submissions. They then use their understanding of the community to review projects and develop funding recommendations. In the Belgium process, selection involved two stages: An independent panel of experts conducted a preliminary assessment against the published selection criteria. A panel of Nike employees evaluated the preselected applications and made the final selection based on the criteria and available budget. Reviewers generally look for detailed and clearly written applications that demonstrate: A well-defined community problem. A clear connection between the problem and the proposed activities. Meaningful benefits for children and young people. Accessible and inclusive implementation. Realistic targets. Measurable results. Appropriate use of the requested funds. Strong partnerships. Potential for lasting impact. A credible plan for continuing or sustaining the work. How to Prepare a Competitive Application Organizations preparing for a future application cycle can take the following steps: Confirm geographic eligibility Verify that the organization and proposed beneficiaries are located within an officially supported community. Review the correct regional rules Do not rely solely on Nike’s general overview. Read the guidelines issued by the regional partner responsible for the relevant location. Confirm the applicant’s legal status Determine whether the organization can apply directly or needs an eligible fiscal sponsor or nonprofit partner. Define the local problem with evidence Explain which young people are excluded from sport, why they are excluded and how the organization knows that the need exists. Connect activities to measurable results State how many children will participate, how frequently activities will take place and what changes the project expects to achieve. Explain accessibility arrangements Address participation costs, transportation, location, equipment, language, disability access, opening hours, safeguarding and registration procedures. Describe coaching quality Explain how coaches will be recruited, trained, supervised and supported to provide a safe and positive experience. Show how girls and underserved young people will be included Identify practical measures for reaching groups that remain underrepresented in sport. Prepare a realistic budget Every major cost should connect directly to a proposed activity or expected result. The requested amount should be proportionate to the number of participants and likely community impact. Document partnerships Include the contribution of schools, community organizations, local authorities, volunteers or other supporters where relevant. Demonstrate sustainability Explain what will remain after the funded period, such as trained coaches, reusable equipment, continuing partnerships, established programs or improved access. Create the online account early New applicants to the Oregon Community Foundation were advised to create their nonprofit account in advance because profile setup and guidance on the next steps could take up to one week. Submit before the regional deadline Applicants should allow enough time for technical problems, missing documents and final internal approval. Reporting Responsibilities Reporting requirements also differ by region. For Pacific Northwest recipients, a report is due by email within one year after the funding is distributed. It must include: The number of children or young people served. Participant information by age and gender. Significant changes made to the project after approval. An impact story describing something achieved, learned or changed for participants. Applicants should therefore design a simple monitoring system before project implementation begins. Attendance records, participant demographics, activity logs, coaching records, photographs obtained with appropriate consent, surveys and beneficiary stories can help demonstrate results. Official Application Information Organizations should begin with the official Nike Community Impact Fund page and select the link for their eligible location. Regional information is available through: King Baudouin Foundation – The Netherlands King Baudouin Foundation – Belgium Oregon Community Foundation – Pacific Northwest Jamaal Magloire Foundation – Toronto Organizations in Atlanta, Mid-South/Memphis and St. Louis should use the Charities Aid Foundation of America link provided on Nike’s official page when a new application round becomes available. Conclusion The Nike Community Impact Fund offers locally rooted organizations an opportunity to expand access to sport and physical activity for children and young people. Its employee-led review system places community knowledge at the centre of funding decisions, while regional partnerships ensure that applications are administered according to local conditions. The strongest applicants will be those that can demonstrate a clear local need, practical removal of participation barriers, inclusive and accessible activities, quality coaching, measurable results, a reasonable budget and a plan for lasting impact. The published 2026 rounds are now closed, and the next application dates have not yet been announced. Interested organizations should prepare their project plans and supporting evidence in advance and begin monitoring the official Nike and regional partner pages around January. title: NASA Open Science Training: Free Open Science Essentials and Open Science 101 Courses
summary: NASA is offering free Open Science training courses designed to help researchers, students, managers, and members of the public develop practical knowledge of open science principles and practices. The training includes Open Science Essentials , a concise introductory course that takes approximately 2 hours , and Open Science 101 , a comprehensive five-module course that takes approximately 12 hours to complete. Both courses are available to the public through NASA’s digital learning platform. Learners can complete the courses at their own pace, and those who successfully complete the training are eligible to receive a digital badge and certificate . About NASA Open Science Training Open science is a collaborative approach to research that promotes the sharing of scientific data, information, tools, knowledge, and results to make research more transparent, accessible, reproducible, and collaborative. NASA describes open science as a culture enabled by technology that supports the sharing of data, information, and knowledge within the scientific community and with the wider public. The NASA Open Science training programme provides learners with practical knowledge they can use to understand and apply open science practices in research. Open Science Essentials Open Science Essentials is designed as a high-level introduction to the principles, practices, and tools associated with open science. The course takes approximately 2 hours to complete and is intended for learners looking for a concise overview of open science concepts. Researchers, managers, and students outside NASA can create an account and register for the course online. The training can be completed at the learner s own pace, with progress saved between sessions. What You Will Learn The Open Science Essentials course covers topics including: The meaning and principles of open science Common challenges and barriers to adopting open science Open data and data ethics Open peer review Collaborative research practices FAIR principles Open Science and Data Management Plans Open-source software Open research results Persistent identifiers Open licensing Repositories and version control Pre-registration The role of artificial intelligence in open science The course is structured into five lessons covering the fundamentals and practical tools needed to begin applying open science approaches. How to Register for Open Science Essentials Researchers, managers, and students outside NASA can register through NASA s online learning platform. Course: Open Science Essentials Duration: Approximately 2 hours Format: Online and self-paced Eligibility: Open to the public Register: NASA Open Science Essentials Open Science 101 Open Science 101 is a more comprehensive training programme for learners who want to develop a deeper understanding of open science and how it can be incorporated into research projects. The course consists of five modules , with the complete training taking approximately 12 hours . Each module takes around 2.5 hours to complete. Like Open Science Essentials, the course is free and self-paced for public learners. What You Will Learn The five modules cover: Module 1: Open Science Fundamentals Explore what open science is, current practices, benefits, and challenges. Module 2: Open Science Tools and Practices Learn about open science fundamentals, including the Use, Make, Share framework, FAIR principles, and essential tools. Module 3: Open Data Learn practical approaches for finding, assessing, creating, and sharing open data. Module 4: Open Code Discover how to apply open-code practices throughout the development lifecycle using the Use, Make, Share framework. Module 5: Open Results and Collaboration Learn how to establish scientific collaborations, develop ethical contributor guidelines, discover and assess open results, and publish and properly credit research outputs. How to Register for Open Science 101 Researchers and students outside NASA can create an account and register for the course through NASA s online learning platform. Course: Open Science 101 Duration: Approximately 12 hours Modules: 5 Format: Online and self-paced Eligibility: Open to the public Register: NASA Open Science 101 Who Can Take the Training? The NASA Open Science courses are available to the general public , including: Researchers Students Scientists Research managers University professionals Early-career researchers Members of the public interested in open science NASA also provides access to the training for its internal workforce through SATERN , the agency s learning management system. Course Certificates and Digital Badges Learners who successfully complete the NASA Open Science training can receive a digital badge and certificate , allowing them to demonstrate their completion of the training and showcase their achievement. Why Open Science Matters Open science promotes greater transparency and collaboration in research. NASA s approach emphasizes making scientific processes and results as open as possible while improving accessibility, reproducibility, and participation. NASA identifies several key principles of open science, including open and transparent research, accessible scientific data and tools, reproducible research, and collaboration among researchers and organizations. The training therefore provides learners with an opportunity to understand how modern research can be conducted and shared more openly. How to Apply for the NASA Open Science Training There is no competitive application process described for the public courses. Interested learners can register directly through NASA s online learning platform . Step 1: Choose a Course Select Open Science Essentials if you want a short introduction to the fundamentals of open science. Choose Open Science 101 if you want a more comprehensive five-module learning experience. Step 2: Create an Account Follow the registration instructions on the relevant NASA course page. Step 3: Complete the Training Both public courses are self-paced, allowing learners to progress through the material according to their own schedule. Step 4: Receive Your Certificate and Digital Badge After successfully completing the course requirements, eligible learners can receive a digital badge and certificate. Conclusion The NASA Open Science Training programme provides free online learning opportunities for researchers, students, managers, and members of the public who want to understand and apply open science practices. With Open Science Essentials providing a two-hour introduction and Open Science 101 offering a deeper five-module learning experience, learners can choose the course that best matches their needs. Those interested in open data, open research, scientific collaboration, research transparency, reproducibility, open-source software, and modern research practices can register through NASA s official training platform. title: UNICEF Club Registration 2026–2027: How to Start or Renew a UNICEF USA Club and Take Action for Children
summary: The UNICEF USA Club Registration for the 2026–2027 school year is now open for students and schools interested in taking action for children in the United States and around the world. The initiative provides an opportunity for students to establish or continue a UNICEF Club and participate in activities that support child rights, awareness, advocacy, fundraising, and UNICEF s broader mission for children. Both new and returning UNICEF Clubs are required to complete the official registration process in order to be recognized as active UNICEF Clubs for the 2026–2027 school year. What Is the UNICEF USA Club Registration? The UNICEF USA Club Registration is the official process through which schools and student groups register a UNICEF Club for the upcoming academic year. UNICEF USA works with communities and young people to build awareness and support for children s rights. Through UNICEF Clubs, students can organize activities and campaigns that help raise awareness about issues affecting children and encourage their peers and communities to become involved. For the 2026–2027 school year , UNICEF USA is inviting both newly established and returning clubs to complete the registration form. Registration is important because a club must be approved by the UNICEF USA team before it can become an active UNICEF Club. Who Should Consider Registering? The registration opportunity is particularly relevant to: Students interested in children s rights and global development. Students who want to organize a UNICEF Club at their school. Existing UNICEF Clubs returning for the 2026–2027 school year. Student leaders interested in advocacy and community engagement. School communities interested in supporting UNICEF s mission. Individuals who want to raise awareness about challenges facing children around the world. Students who want practical experience in leadership, organization, communication, teamwork, advocacy, and community activities. Whether you are establishing a UNICEF Club for the first time or continuing an existing club, UNICEF USA states that both new and returning clubs must complete the registration form . What Can a UNICEF Club Do? A UNICEF Club can provide students with a structured platform to become involved in issues affecting children. Depending on the activities organized by a particular club, students may have opportunities to: Raise awareness about children s rights. Educate fellow students about challenges affecting children. Organize school or community activities. Support UNICEF-related campaigns. Encourage advocacy for children. Participate in fundraising or awareness initiatives. Develop leadership and organizational skills. Work collaboratively with other students and an advisor. Engage their school community around issues affecting children. Connect local student action with UNICEF s work for children around the world. The club structure can therefore be particularly valuable for students who want to combine education, leadership and community involvement. Requirements Before Starting the Registration One of the most important things prospective applicants should know is that the registration form requires information about the club s leadership and advisor. UNICEF USA requires the contact information of: Four club leaders One club advisor Applicants should therefore collect all necessary contact information before starting the registration form . This is especially important because UNICEF USA states that there is no save-and-return option on the registration form. In other words, applicants should make sure they have the required information available before beginning the application. Information You Should Prepare Before accessing the registration form, prospective clubs should have the details of their four club leaders and one advisor ready. It is advisable to verify the information carefully before submitting the form to avoid unnecessary delays or mistakes. Applicants should also make sure that everyone involved understands their role within the club and is prepared to provide accurate contact information. UNICEF Club Registration Process The UNICEF USA registration page contains a multi-stage webform. The registration process is organized into several sections. According to the registration page, applicants will move through the following stages: 1. Find Your School or Organization The first stage involves identifying the school or organization associated with the UNICEF Club. Applicants should provide the requested information so UNICEF USA can associate the club with the appropriate educational institution or organization. 2. Get Started After identifying the school or organization, applicants proceed to the next stage of the registration process. This section begins the formal club registration questionnaire. 3. Questionnaire Applicants will complete the questionnaire provided as part of the UNICEF Club registration process. It is important to read each question carefully and provide accurate information. 4. Advisor Information The registration process requires information about the club s advisor. As noted by UNICEF USA, each club must provide information for one advisor . Prospective clubs should therefore have their advisor s required information available before starting. 5. Enter Your Leader Information This section requires information about the club s student leaders. UNICEF USA requires contact information for four club leaders . Clubs should therefore select their leadership team and collect the required information before beginning the registration form. 6.
